Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/Zuma Press/Rex/Shutterstock Arron Banks Arron Banks hired private investigators to dig into Conservative party chair Revelation comes after it was disclosed that Reform UK backer had paid for spying on prominent journalist Rowena Mason Whitehall editor Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 12.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The businessman and Reform UK backer Arron Banks commissioned a private intelligence firm to dig into the Conservative party chair, in addition to having paid for an investigation into a prominent journalist. Banks, a former Reform UK candidate and leave campaign donor, appeared to confirm on Sunday that he was behind an investigation into Kevin Hollinrake. The use of private investigators to look into Hollinrake was first reported by the Mail on Sunday, which said Banks had used Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he previously owned. As party chair, Hollinrake has led the Conservatives’ response to revelations about Nigel Farage’s finances, asking questions about the £5m undeclared gift Farage received from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election. Hollinrake addressed Banks on social media on Sunday, saying: “When you can’t answer the questions, investigate the people asking them. After we called for scrutiny of Reform UK’s finances, a close associate of Nigel Farage reportedly hired private investigators to dig into me (and journalists covering the same story).” In a reply on X, Banks said: “I’ve always come across people in this world who like to give it but can’t receive it.” Pressed on whether Reform knew about the surveillance, Banks suggested he had acted alone, saying: “I row my own boat.” Banks has been approached by the Guardian for comment. View image in fullscreen Kevin Hollinrake has been leading the Conservatives’ response to revelations about Nigel Farage’s finances. Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/Zuma Press/Rex/Shutterstock The developments come after it emerged previously in the New Statesman that Banks had commissioned Precision Risk to investigate Gabriel Pogrund, the investigations editor of the Sunday Times. The revelation led to fears that other journalists examining the funding of Reform and Farage, including those at the Guardian, could have been targeted. When asked previously whether he had commissioned investigators to surveil reporters at the Guardian, Banks said he was “not really interested in the Guardian” but declined to comment further. The News Media Association (NMA), which represents regional and national media, raised concerns and described it as an “attack on our democracy”. The Guardian, along with the Sunday Times, has broken a series of stories in recent months revealing how cash has been given to Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors. Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the NMA, said aggressive attempts to deter journalistic inquiry were at risk of becoming normalised. He said: “Using private investigators to try to deter journalists from making legitimate inquiries about public figures is an attack on our democracy. Sadly, intimidation and abuse of local and national journalists is increasingly used as a weapon to limit scrutiny and deflect attention away from matters of public interest. This must not become normalised. “Ministers must wake up to this threat to our democracy and do much more to protect the independent journalism which underpins our democratic way of life.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Banks previously told the New Statesman: “We believe the Sunday Times used hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.” The Sunday Times has rejected Banks’s suggestion. Banks, when asked directly by the New Statesman whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, responded: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.” The Sunday Times published a new investigation this weekend into links between Reform funders and Tether.bet, a website accused of illegally offering gambling to UK punters, which closed this week. The newspaper said the convicted fraudster George Cottrell was a high-profile customer of the website, and Harborne owned a company, IFX, that processed payments on behalf of another company that took deposits and returned winnings. Cottrell’s lawyers told the newspaper his relationship with Tether.bet “has been limited to that of a customer, in addition to which he knows and is friends with the owner”. When contacted by the Guardian, Cottrell’s lawyers said he was one of the world’s best-known professional gamblers. “It is therefore hardly surprising that [others] may seek to associate themselves with him in an attempt to lend credibility to their businesses or generate publicity. Mr Cottrell has never invested in, owned or operated any betting company or casino. He has never solicited clients for any betting company or casino. Any suggestion that he was involved in unlawful gambling activity is wholly false.” Harborne and IFX’s representatives told the Sunday Times he had never had any role in the running and operations of IFX and that it “operates in accordance with applicable regulations and legislation across the markets it supports”. A Labour spokesperson said in response: “These reports raise yet more questions about the people bankrolling Reform and Nigel Farage … Farage cannot run from the truth for ever. The mountain of unanswered questions around his finances and judgment is only getting bigger. He needs stop the excuses, come clean with the public.” Explore more on these topics Arron Banks Reform UK Conservatives Investigative journalism Newspapers news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgj.text: Figure caption, Watch: Bystander who stopped Oregon school shooter describes how he approached gunman By Shaimaa Khalil North America Correspondent Published 23 October 2026 A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives". Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco. "I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday. "The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save." Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them". He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life. "I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said. The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded. Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day. The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began. He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school. Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services. "I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster. He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building. "I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Three schoolchildren and a teacher were killed in the shooting Giamanco crawled through a shattered window and reached the classroom, where a teacher was locked in a struggle with the gunman. He opened the door and fired. Giamanco told OPB he fired again when the attacker reached for his weapon. He then placed his own gun on the ground and raised his hands as an officer appeared. He described feeling like the "last line of defence" between the children and the gunman, and said he "was supposed to be there" that day. Afterwards, he called his wife to say he would not be home for lunch and that she needed to get to the school immediately. He then called his mother to tell her what had happened. "Mum, I just had to take the life of what I think is might be a child because he ran into my daughter's school with a gun," he said. Police identified the gunman as Griffin J John II - a former pupil who had attended special education classes at the school. His motive remains under investigation. Police said the teacher who confronted the attacker had thrown her phone at him, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed". The youngest victim was Rhoam Summer, aged five. His father said the family was "broken and lost". Megan Lambert, 25, the teacher who was killed, was working in what her family described as her "dream job". "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said. The other two boys have not been publicly named at their families' request. The injured teacher has been named as Becky Drury, 54. She said i n a statement shared with US media that the gunman shot her as she tried to shut her classroom door. Children aged 5, 8 and 11 killed in US school shooting before suspect shot by bystander Published 16 October Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive Published 1 day ago Giamanco's name became public less than a day after the shooting. His mother, Kenda Freeman, read a family statement saying he was not seeking recognition and asking for privacy. Shortly after the attack, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised his intervention while acknowledging its emotional cost. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well," she said. Giamanco told OPB he now lies awake after his family goes to bed, replaying the attack. "I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams."
